Step-By-Step: How To Measure And Mark The Perfect Hanging Height

Right — let us get practical. This is the process I use every single time I hang art in a client's home, whether it is one piece or twenty. It removes the guesswork entirely, and it means you only ever make the holes you actually need.

You will need: a tape measure, a pencil, a spirit level (or a free spirit level app on your phone), and a piece of painter's tape. That is genuinely all.

Step-by-step measuring method

  • Step 1 — Measure your art: Measure the full height of the piece (frame included if framed). Divide by two to find the centre point of the art
  • Step 2 — Find the hanging hardware distance: Flip the art over and measure from the top of the frame down to the hanging wire or hook at its tightest point (when pulled taut). Note this measurement
  • Step 3 — Calculate the nail position: Your nail should go in at: your desired centre height (e.g. 57 inches from floor) MINUS the hardware distance from Step 2. This is the nail height from the floor
  • Step 4 — Mark the spot: Use painter's tape to mark the exact nail position on the wall. Double-check with your tape measure
  • Step 5 — Check level: If hanging more than one piece, use your spirit level to ensure multiple nail marks are perfectly horizontal
  • Step 6 — Reality check: Before you put the nail in, hold the art up at the marked position and step back. Look at it. Check it relates correctly to any furniture beneath. Adjust the tape mark if needed
  • Step 7 — Hang: Put the nail or hook in at the marked spot. Hang the art. Check with a spirit level that it is straight. Step back and enjoy
Pro Tip: For art with a picture wire rather than a fixed hook, the wire sags to a different depth depending on where the nail lands. Always measure the wire pulled tight at the exact centre of the frame — not at the edges — to get an accurate hardware distance for Step 2.

If you want to go deeper on the 57-inch rule and the thinking behind it, the team at Apartment Therapy have a clear and practical breakdown worth reading — including the classic How High to Hang a Picture? Ready To Finally Hang Your Art With Confidence?

I hope this guide has taken some of the anxiety out of what should be one of the most enjoyable parts of making your apartment feel like home. The measurements and rules are genuinely useful, but the most important thing is to trust your eye once you have done the groundwork.

Measure carefully, use the paper template trick before committing any holes, always check the relationship between your art and the furniture beneath it, and adjust for your ceiling height and furniture scale. Do those four things and you will almost always get it right.

Your apartment walls are one of the most powerful tools you have for making a rented, or even just temporary, space feel completely and genuinely yours. Do not leave your art on the floor any longer than you have to.

How long does apartment decorating take? Honestly, it depends — but most people can get from bare walls to a space that genuinely feels like home in anywhere from four weeks to six months, depending on their budget, the size of their flat, and how much they plan ahead. The good news? With the right approach, you can make a serious dent in the first weekend.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever moved into a new flat, looked around at the empty white walls, and felt that slightly sinking feeling — like the place could be anywhere and belong to nobody? I get that question from clients all the time, and it usually comes with a second question: how long is this going to take? The answer starts with wall art — it's almost always the quickest, most impactful change you can make to a bare room.

Quick answer: Apartment decorating typically takes between four weeks and six months from move-in to a fully finished space. Most people style one room at a time, with wall decor and art being the fastest way to make any room feel complete. A structured, week-by-week plan cuts that timeline down significantly.

When I talk about apartment decorating, I mean the whole process — from choosing a colour palette right through to hanging the last piece of unique wall art and styling your shelves with unique home decor. It's not just about furniture. It's about layering — adding personality, warmth, and visual interest until a space stops feeling like a rental and starts feeling like yours.

How Long Does Apartment Decorating Actually Take by Room

Every room has a different rhythm when it comes to decorating, and knowing that upfront saves a lot of frustration. The living room almost always takes longest because it's the most layered space — furniture, lighting, rugs, shelving, and wall art all have to work together.

Bedrooms can come together surprisingly quickly if you focus on the bed first and treat it as the anchor. Kitchens and bathrooms are usually the fastest because there's less surface area to style and fewer decisions to make.

Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. Rough Time Estimates by Room

  • Living room: 3–8 weeks (most decisions, most layers)
  • Bedroom: 2–4 weeks (anchor on the bed, then build outward)
  • Kitchen: 1–2 weeks (functional first, styling second)
  • Bathroom: 1–2 weeks (accessories and mirrors make the biggest difference)
  • Hallway / entryway: 1 week (often overlooked but quick to style)
  • Home office: 2–3 weeks (desk setup, lighting, and one or two wall pieces)

I once helped a client who'd been in her one-bed flat for eight months and still hadn't touched the bedroom walls. She assumed the bedroom was "done" because she had a bed and some curtains. Once we added a floating shelf, a couple of ceramic pieces, and sorted the bedside lighting, the room completely transformed — and it took us one afternoon.

Pro Tip: Don't try to decorate every room at once. Pick the room you spend the most time in and get it to 80% finished before moving on. You'll feel less overwhelmed, and you'll make better decisions.

Factors That Affect Your Decorating Timeline (Budget, Style, Size)

If you're wondering how long does apartment decorating take for your specific situation, three things matter more than anything else: your budget, the size of your flat, and whether you have a clear style in mind. Get those sorted early and everything else flows faster.

Budget is the biggest variable. If you're working with a tight budget, you'll naturally spread purchases over a longer period — which is fine, but it means your space will be in an "in progress" state for longer. A clearer style direction means fewer wasted purchases and fewer do-overs.

A Realistic Decorating Timeline: From Move-In to Finished Space

A realistic decorating timeline for most apartments runs from four weeks at the very fastest (for a studio flat with a clear style and a decent budget) to six months for a larger flat being decorated gradually. The middle ground — a one or two-bed flat, moderate budget — is usually two to three months.

The mistake I always see is people trying to make everything perfect in the first week, then burning out and leaving the flat half-finished for months. A phased approach is far more effective and honestly far more enjoyable.

A Black British man in his late twenties, wearing a grey t-shirt and jeans, kneeling on the floor unpacking a box of books in a natural candid pose.]]

The Three Phases of Apartment Decorating

  • Phase 1 — Foundations (Weeks 1–2): Furniture placement, curtains, rugs, and basic lighting. The essentials that make a space liveable.
  • Phase 2 — Character (Weeks 3–6): Shelving, mirrors, plants, and secondary lighting. The pieces that add depth.
  • Phase 3 — Personality (Weeks 6–12+): Wall art, curated accessories, textiles, and the finishing touches that make the space unmistakably yours.

I had a client who moved into a new flat and insisted on getting everything done in two weeks. By week three she'd returned half of what she'd bought, because nothing felt cohesive — she'd been choosing things in a rush without a clear palette. We stripped it back, agreed on a warm neutral base with terracotta accents, and rebuilt from there. The second attempt took six weeks and felt completely different — calm, intentional, and genuinely beautiful.

Real Example: A client decorating a two-bed flat in Manchester spread her purchases over 10 weeks using a simple phased checklist. Her living room was "finished" by week four, the bedroom by week seven, and the second room and hallway by week ten. She spent less overall because she stopped impulse-buying.

Your Week-by-Week Apartment Decorating Schedule

This is the section most decorating guides miss entirely — a proper, actionable schedule you can actually follow. I've used a version of this with dozens of clients and it genuinely works, whether you're in a studio or a two-bedroom flat.

The key is treating each week as a single decision-making focus. Don't try to tackle everything at once. Small, consistent progress beats one chaotic shopping weekend every time.

[[IMG|week-by-week-decorating-schedule-apartment|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Your Week-by-Week Decorating Schedule". Then a clear vertical timeline with 8 labelled steps, each with a small icon: Week 1: "Measure & plan" (ruler icon); Week 2: "Furniture in place" (sofa icon); Week 3: "Rugs, curtains, lighting" (lamp icon); Week 4: "Mirrors & shelves" (mirror icon); Week 5: "Plants & textiles" (leaf icon); Week 6: "Wall art & hangings" (picture frame outline icon); Week 7: "Accessories & styling" (vase icon); Week 8: "Final tweaks & done" (tick icon). Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Week-by-Week Breakdown

  • Week 1: Measure every room. Photograph blank walls. Create a mood board (Pinterest or physical). Decide on your main colour palette.
  • Week 2: Arrange your main furniture. Don't buy anything new yet — live with what you have and see what's actually missing.
  • Week 3: Source and hang curtains or blinds. Lay down the main rug in the living room. Sort your key overhead lighting.
  • Week 4: Add mirrors (they open up small spaces dramatically). Put up any floating shelves you want. Add a floor lamp or two for warmth.
  • Week 5: Introduce plants — even two or three make a room feel alive. Layer in textiles: throw cushions, a blanket, towels in the bathroom.
  • Week 6: This is the wall art week. Choose pieces that feel personal. Don't default to whatever was on sale — this is where the flat starts feeling like you.
  • Week 7: Style your shelves and surfaces. Group objects in odd numbers. Add candles, books, small ceramic pieces.
  • Week 8: Step back and review. What feels off? What's missing? Make one or two final edits — not a whole new shopping list.
Pro Tip: Week 6 is wall art week for a reason — walls are the last layer, not the first. If you hang art before you've placed furniture, you'll almost certainly end up repositioning it. Save yourself the wall damage and wait until your furniture layout is locked in.

Should You Decorate Fast or Slow? Pros and Cons

This is genuinely a matter of personal style — and I don't mean your interior style, I mean how you make decisions. Some people do their best work with a deadline and a big shopping weekend. Others need to sit with a space for a while before they know what it needs.

Neither approach is wrong. But there are real trade-offs to both, and being honest with yourself about which type you are will save you money and frustration.

Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. Scene: a side-by-side feel — on the left half of the frame, a living room corner that feels sparse and unfinished (a plain sofa, no accessories, empty walls except for a macramé hanging); on the right half, the same corner styled fully with a floor lamp, trailing potted plant, a woven basket, and a decorative mirror leaning against the wall. Warm natural evening light. A mixed-race couple — a woman with natural curly hair and a man with a warm olive complexion — sitting on the sofa together, the woman gesturing toward the styled side of the room in a candid, conversational pose.]]
Decorating Fast Decorating Slowly
Pros Space feels finished quickly; motivating; clear deadline More considered choices; less waste; better budget control
Cons Risk of impulse buys; harder to return things; can feel chaotic Living in an unfinished space for months; loss of momentum
Best for People with a clear style, decisive nature, and a reasonable budget People still discovering their style, or working with a tight budget
Pro Tip: If you're somewhere in between — you want speed but also care about getting it right — use the phased approach and give yourself a hard deadline for each phase. Treat it like a project with milestones, not a vague ongoing task.

How to Prioritise What to Decorate First in a New Apartment

When you're starting from scratch, it can feel like everything needs doing at once, which leads to paralysis — or worse, panic-buying things you don't really love. The rule I give every new client is simple: start with what you see most, use most, and spend the most time in.

For most people, that's the living room followed by the bedroom. Everything else — the kitchen, bathroom, hallway — can wait a few extra weeks without affecting how you feel day to day.

[[IMG|what-to-decorate-first-new-apartment|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. Scene: a cosy living room in a rental apartment that is clearly in the process of being styled — a cream boucle sofa with a rust-coloured throw over one arm, a round wooden coffee table with a candle and a small stack of books, a jute rug beneath it, a woven wall hanging mounted on the wall, a large potted fiddle-leaf fig in the corner. Soft warm afternoon light. A woman of East Asian heritage in her early thirties, wearing an oversized cream knit jumper, sitting cross-legged on the sofa with a notebook on her lap, appearing to make notes or decisions in a natural candid pose.]]

Your Decorating Priority Order

  • 1. Living room: It sets the tone for the whole flat. Get the sofa, rug, and lighting sorted first.
  • 2. Bedroom: Good sleep matters. Invest in proper bedding and window coverings early.
  • 3. Entryway / hallway: This is the first thing you see when you come home. Even a mirror and a hook rail make it feel welcoming.
  • 4. Kitchen: Add small accessories — a plant on the windowsill, a tea towel, a small piece of wall art — but save bigger kitchen styling for later.
  • 5. Bathroom: A good mirror and matching accessories go a long way. This can be last on the list without much impact.
Real Example: A client who moved into a two-bed flat in Bristol spent her first two weeks entirely on the living room. By week three it was genuinely finished — and that one room gave her the confidence and clarity to tackle everything else efficiently. She later said it was the best decorating decision she ever made.

Wall Art and Decor Layering as Your Final-Stage Strategy

Wall art is almost always a final-stage decision, and that's actually a good thing. By the time you're ready to hang something on the walls, you know your furniture layout, your colour palette, and what the room actually needs — which means you're far more likely to get it right first time.

Layering is the professional approach: you start with the largest, heaviest elements (furniture, rugs) and work your way up to the lightest, most personal layers (art, small accessories, plants). Walls are the canvas for that final, personal layer.

[[IMG|wall-art-decor-layering-final-stage|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. Scene: a beautifully layered living room wall — a long floating shelf mounted at eye height, styled with small ceramic vases, a trailing potted plant, a small sculptural object, and a geometric macramé hanging above it; below the shelf a curved cream sofa with layered cushions in terracotta and sage. Warm diffused natural light from the left. A Nigerian-British woman in her late twenties, wearing a sage green blouse, standing to the side of the shelf and carefully placing a small ceramic piece in a natural, considered pose.]]

How to Layer Wall Decor Effectively

  • Layer 1 — Paint or wall colour: The base. Even in a rental, a feature wall in a removable colour or textured wallpaper can transform a room.
  • Layer 2 — Large structural pieces: Mirrors, floating shelves, wall-mounted lighting or sconces.
  • Layer 3 — Textile elements: Macramé hangings, woven tapestries, fabric panels. These add softness and texture.
  • Layer 4 — Wall art: Prints, canvases, or a gallery arrangement. This is where personality comes through most strongly.
  • Layer 5 — Small accents: Plants in hanging pots, small sculptural wall objects, decorative hooks.

Here's what happened when I tried doing this in reverse on my own flat: I hung a gallery wall before I'd settled on the sofa position. When the sofa finally arrived and went against a different wall, the whole gallery arrangement looked completely wrong — too far to one side, out of proportion. I had to patch and rehang everything. It was a two-hour job that could have been a twenty-minute one if I'd waited.

Pro Tip: Before you hang anything on the walls, cut out paper templates in the exact size of each piece and tape them to the wall with painter's tape. Live with the layout for a day before you put a single nail in. It saves a lot of unnecessary wall damage — especially important in rented flats.

Cost-Per-Phase Breakdown to Manage Your Decorating Budget Over Time

One of the biggest reasons apartment decorating drags on longer than it should is poor budget planning. People spend too much in the first week on furniture and then have nothing left for the finishing touches — which, ironically, are the things that make a space feel done.

I always suggest thinking of your total decorating budget in thirds: roughly a third on furniture and large pieces, a third on lighting, rugs, curtains, and shelving, and a final third on art, accessories, and finishing touches. That last third is the one that gets cut — and it shows.

[[IMG|decorating-budget-phases-breakdown|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "How to Split Your Decorating Budget". Then three clearly labelled horizontal bars arranged vertically, like a simple bar chart: Bar 1 labelled "Phase 1 – Furniture & Foundations" at roughly 35% width; Bar 2 labelled "Phase 2 – Lighting, Rugs & Shelving" at roughly 35% width; Bar 3 labelled "Phase 3 – Art, Accessories & Finishing" at roughly 30% width. Each bar a different shade of grey. Below each bar a short note: "Sofas, beds, wardrobes"; "Curtains, lamps, floating shelves"; "Wall art, plants, ceramics". Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Rough Budget Split by Phase

  • Phase 1 — Foundations: Approximately 35% of total budget. Sofa, bed frame, wardrobe, dining table. These are your anchor investments.
  • Phase 2 — Character layers: Approximately 35% of total budget. Curtains, rugs, lamps, floating shelves, mirrors. This is where the room starts to breathe.
  • Phase 3 — Personality and finishing: Approximately 30% of total budget. Wall art, plants, ceramics, throws, candles, books. Don't cut this phase — it's the most visible.

I worked with a couple decorating their first flat together, and they'd spent almost all their budget in the first two phases. By the time we got to wall art and accessories, they had very little left. We got creative — a few thoughtfully chosen prints, a couple of trailing plants from a garden centre, and some ceramic pieces sourced from a local market. It looked deliberate and personal, not budget-constrained. The lesson: even a small Phase 3 budget, spent wisely, makes an enormous difference.

Pro Tip: Write your full decorating wish list, then assign every item to one of the three phases before you spend a penny. Knowing which phase each item belongs to makes it much easier to say "not yet" without feeling like you're giving up on it entirely.
[[PRODUCT|ceramic and sculptural home decor accessories]]

Common Mistakes That Make Decorating Take Longer Than It Should

After twelve years of helping people style their homes, I've seen the same mistakes come up again and again. None of them are catastrophic — but they all add weeks (sometimes months) to the process, and most of them are completely avoidable.

The single biggest time-waster? Not measuring before buying. I cannot tell you how many clients have ordered a sofa that wouldn't fit through the door, or a rug that was swamped by the room. Measure twice, order once — it really is that simple.

[[IMG|common-decorating-mistakes-apartment|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. Scene: a slightly chaotic but relatable apartment living room in the middle of a decorating project — a tape measure on the floor, a notepad with scribbled measurements on the coffee table, a rug that appears slightly too small for the space, an empty wall with just a single macramé hanging slightly off-centre. Warm natural light. A white British man in his mid-thirties wearing a checked shirt and jeans, crouching down next to the rug with a tape measure in hand, looking mildly exasperated in a genuine candid pose.]]

The Most Common Decorating Mistakes

  • Not measuring: Every piece of furniture and every rug needs to be measured against your actual room dimensions before you buy.
  • Choosing a style mid-process: If you don't know your style before you start shopping, you'll end up with a mix of things that don't work together.
  • Buying too much at once: Rooms need time to breathe between additions. Add pieces gradually to see what the space actually needs.
  • Decorating walls too early: Hang art before your furniture is settled and you'll almost certainly move it. Save the walls for last.
  • Ignoring lighting: A poorly lit room will never feel finished, no matter how much you spend on everything else. Lighting is as important as any piece of furniture.
  • Choosing based on trend, not personal taste: Trends change. Your home should reflect you, not a passing mood board moment.
  • Neglecting the entryway: The hallway sets the tone the moment you walk in. Don't leave it bare and unloved.
Real Example: A client in Leeds spent three months redecorating because she'd bought everything in one weekend without a colour plan. Nothing worked together, and she ended up returning about 60% of what she'd bought. The second time around, she spent one week on a mood board and a colour palette — and the whole flat came together in six weeks with almost no returns.

How to Make an Apartment Feel Finished Quickly With Minimal Pieces

Sometimes you just need the flat to feel like a home as quickly as possible — whether you've just moved in, you're hosting people next week, or you simply can't face months of ongoing decorating. The good news is that a handful of well-chosen pieces can make a space feel genuinely complete, even if it isn't technically "finished" yet.

The secret is contrast and warmth. An empty room feels cold and hard. Add a rug, a light source that isn't overhead, a plant, and something on the walls — and the whole feeling of the space shifts. You don't need twenty pieces. You need five good ones.

[[IMG|make-apartment-feel-finished-minimal-pieces|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal / Japandi styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome and encouraged — shelves, macramé hangings, wall lighting/sconces, mirrors, hanging plants — style the walls naturally and lived-in. Scene: a beautifully minimal but complete-feeling studio apartment — a cream linen sofa, a simple jute rug, a large round mirror leaning against one wall, a floor lamp with a warm bulb casting golden evening light, a large trailing pothos plant in a terracotta pot in the corner, and a single woven wall hanging above the sofa. The overall feeling is calm, warm, and intentional. A woman of Middle Eastern heritage in her late twenties, wearing a soft blush-toned wrap dress, curled on the sofa with a mug in hand, in a natural, relaxed candid pose.]]

The Five Pieces That Make Any Room Feel Finished

  • 1. A rug: The single most transformative piece in any room. It grounds the space and defines zones.
  • 2. A non-overhead light source: A floor lamp or table lamp in the corner changes the entire mood of a room, especially in the evening.
  • 3. A mirror: It adds light, depth, and visual interest — especially in smaller flats where space is at a premium.
  • 4. A plant (or two): A large indoor plant in the corner of a room makes it feel alive and cared for instantly.
  • 5. Something on the wall: One considered wall piece — a macramé hanging, a woven textile, or a well-chosen art print — anchors the room and makes it feel personal.
Pro Tip: If you're in a rush and can only do one thing — do the lighting. Switching off the overhead light and turning on a warm floor lamp transforms a flat, stark room into something that feels genuinely welcoming. It costs almost nothing and takes five minutes.
[[PRODUCT|floor lamps and ambient lighting for home styling]]

Apartment Decorating Styles: Visual Ideas to Help You Plan

Sometimes the best way to nail down your decorating direction is simply to see what different finished spaces actually look like — not mood boards, but real rooms styled from the ground up. Whether you're drawn to warm Japandi minimalism, maximalist colour, or something cosier and more eclectic, having a visual reference makes every decision faster and more confident.

Visual Inspiration

Explore complementary design ideas on our Home Decor by Trend page:

  • Cosy Minimalism Home Decor Trend - Simple walls styled with ease
  • Modern Contemporary Home Decor Trend - Clean apartment walls done quickly
  • Transitional Interior Design Trend - Versatile decor for any timeline

More on Decorating Timelines: What the Research Actually Says

Most decorating guides online wildly underestimate how long a real decorating project takes — and it's worth understanding why, so you can plan more realistically.

The "HGTV myth" — the idea that a whole home can be transformed over a weekend — has genuinely distorted how people approach decorating. As explored in How Long Does A Decorating Project Take: The HGTV Myth, real decorating projects take far longer than TV suggests, because they involve decision fatigue, delivery lead times, returns, and the natural process of learning what a space actually needs.

The practical takeaway from all of this is that a well-planned, phased approach — one that gives you space to learn as you go — will always produce a better result than a rushed all-in-one effort. That's true whether you're decorating a studio flat or a larger home.

Give yourself permission for the process to take as long as it takes. The goal isn't a fast finish. The goal is a space you genuinely love.

WATCH: Wall Decor Ideas in Action

WATCH: 15 Wall Decor Ideas For Your Home | Apartment Therapy

Ready to Start? Here's My Final Word

Wherever you are in the process — whether you moved in last week or you've been living with bare walls for two years — it's never too late to start, and there's no single right way to do it.

The best approach is the one you'll actually stick to. Whether that's a disciplined week-by-week schedule or a slower, more organic build, what matters is that each piece you add makes the space feel a little more like you.

Start with what you spend the most time in. Get the lighting right before you do almost anything else. Save the walls for last — and when you're ready for them, choose things that feel genuinely personal, not just things that were on trend or on sale.

Your flat doesn't need to be finished to feel like a home. It just needs a few things in it that you actually love.

Finding the right wall art for Scandinavian furniture is one of those things that sounds simple until you're standing in your living room holding a print, wondering why it looks completely wrong next to your pale oak sideboard. The good news is there's a clear logic to it — and once you understand it, every choice gets much easier.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever bought a print you absolutely loved, hung it up with high hopes, and then felt vaguely disappointed — like something was slightly off but you couldn't quite put your finger on it? That's one of the most common struggles I hear from people decorating Nordic-style spaces, and it's almost always fixable. If you're not sure where to begin, browsing some well-curated wall art options designed for modern interiors is a genuinely useful starting point.

Quick answer: Wall art that complements Scandinavian furniture tends to be clean, minimal, and rooted in nature — think botanical prints, abstract line art, black-and-white photography, or simple typographic pieces in neutral or muted tones. Pair them with thin natural wood or matte black frames, keep the scale generous, and stick to a tight palette of two or three colours already present in your furniture. That combination works in almost every room.

Scandinavian interior design is built on a belief that everyday spaces should feel calm, functional, and genuinely pleasant to live in — not just look nice in photos. It favours natural materials like oak and birch, a restrained neutral palette, and carefully chosen objects that earn their place. When you're adding unique wall art to a Scandi-style room, you're not just decorating a blank wall — you're choosing something that needs to sit quietly and confidently alongside furniture that doesn't shout. The same applies to unique home decor more broadly: every piece should feel intentional rather than accidental.

List of Contents

  • What is Scandinavian Wall Art and Its Defining Style Characteristics
  • Best Wall Art Types to Pair with Scandinavian Furniture
  • How to Choose the Right Prints, Colours and Frames for a Nordic Interior
  • Room-by-Room Styling Guide for Scandinavian Furniture Pairings
  • How to Mix Wall Art with Specific Scandi Furniture Brands Like IKEA or HAY
  • Sizing and Gallery Wall Layout Tips for Minimalist Scandi Spaces

  • More About Scandinavian Interior Design and Wall Art Styling

What is Scandinavian Wall Art and Its Defining Style Characteristics

Scandinavian wall art isn't a single fixed category — it's a sensibility. It refers to artwork that reflects the same values as Nordic interior design: simplicity, restraint, natural references, and a quiet kind of beauty that doesn't need to announce itself.

The style emerged from countries like Denmark, Sweden, Norway, and Finland, where long winters and limited daylight pushed designers to create interiors that felt warm and light simultaneously. That tension — cosy but never cluttered, warm but never fussy — is what defines the aesthetic at its best.

[[IMG|scandinavian-wall-art-style-characteristics|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor is welcome — include a simple wooden wall shelf holding small ceramics and a trailing plant. A bright Scandinavian-style living room with pale birch flooring, a low-profile linen sofa in warm oat, a round oak coffee table with a ceramic vase, and soft diffused window light casting gentle shadows. Include a South Asian woman in her early thirties sitting cross-legged on the sofa, reading a book with a relaxed expression, wearing a soft cream knitted jumper.]]

Core characteristics of Scandinavian wall art

  • Minimal composition: Lots of negative space, clean lines, uncluttered subjects.
  • Nature-led motifs: Plants, animals, landscapes, forests, and water.
  • Muted or natural colour palettes: Warm whites, soft greys, dusty greens, terracotta, and charcoal.
  • Graphic simplicity: Bold shapes, thin lines, and strong contrast without complexity.
  • Typographic prints: Short words or quotes in clean sans-serif or hand-lettered fonts.
  • Black-and-white photography: Landscapes, architecture, or portraits with strong tonal contrast.

I once helped a client who'd furnished her entire flat in classic Scandinavian pieces — pale wood, linen, neutral ceramics — and then hung a large maximalist floral painting she'd inherited. She loved the painting but it felt jarring. We didn't ditch it; we moved it to a gallery wall alongside simpler line art pieces that gave it breathing room. The trick was framing everything in the same matte white, which created enough visual consistency that the bold painting became a focal point rather than an accident.

Pro Tip: If you're unsure whether a piece suits a Nordic interior, ask yourself: does it feel calm when you look at it? If the answer is yes, it very likely fits.

Best Wall Art Types to Pair with Scandinavian Furniture

Some art types just work instinctively in Scandi-style rooms, and others almost always clash — not because they're inferior art, but because they're speaking a different visual language to the furniture around them.

The furniture itself tends to be structured, low-profile, and made from natural materials. You want art that responds to those qualities rather than fights them.

[[IMG|best-wall-art-types-scandinavian-furniture|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal styling. Natural soft light, no text, logos or watermarks. Do NOT add framed wall art, prints or pictures on the walls. Other wall decor welcome — include a wall-mounted wooden shelf and a simple macramé hanging. A Nordic-style study or reading nook with a compact oak desk, a warm-toned linen chair, a small potted olive tree in a terracotta pot, and a simple wooden wall shelf displaying small objects. Include a Black British man in his mid-forties sitting at the desk writing in a notebook, looking thoughtful, wearing a muted navy shirt.]]

Best-performing art types for Scandi interiors

  • Botanical line art: Simple single-line drawings of plants, leaves, or seeds. Works with almost any Scandi furniture.
  • Abstract minimalist prints: Geometric shapes, soft colour-block washes, or fluid forms in two to three colours.
  • Black-and-white photography: Architectural shots, Nordic landscapes, or close-up nature photography.
  • Typographic prints: Single words, short phrases, or coordinates in a clean typeface — keep fonts simple.
  • Textured textile art: Woven wall hangings or macramé pieces add warmth without breaking the minimal aesthetic.
  • Watercolour botanicals: Soft washes in sage, dusty pink, or warm grey pair beautifully with pale oak.
  • Maps and city prints: In a simple line style, these feel at home above a Scandinavian-style desk or console.
[[PRODUCT|minimal botanical line art prints for Scandinavian interiors]]
Pro Tip: Textile wall hangings — woven or macramé — are one of the most underused options in Scandi rooms. They add texture without adding visual noise, and they work beautifully above beds or sofas where a framed print might feel too rigid.

How to Choose the Right Prints, Colours and Frames for a Nordic Interior

This is where most people go slightly wrong, and it's nearly always about colour. The print itself might be perfect, but if the frame is the wrong tone or the colours in the artwork pull in a direction the room isn't going, the whole thing feels off.

Scandinavian interiors work in a fairly tight colour window — and that's actually your friend, because it makes decisions clearer once you know the rules.

[[IMG|prints-colours-frames-nordic-interior|3:2|infographic|Clean minimal educational infographic, plain WHITE background, photoreal, all text solid BLACK. A short centred title near the top reading "Choosing Prints, Colours & Frames for Nordic Interiors". Then a clear visual comparison: on the left, a labelled example showing a warm-toned Scandi room with a pale oak frame and muted botanical print labelled "Works Well"; on the right, a labelled example showing the same room setting with a heavily ornate gold frame and a bold jewel-toned print labelled "Avoid". Below each, three bullet-point labels noting key reasons. Minimal words, generous white space, nothing near the edges. No people, no watermarks.]]

Colour and frame pairing guide

Furniture Tone Recommended Art Colours Best Frame Choices Frames to Avoid
Pale / light oak Warm whites, sage, dusty terracotta, soft grey Natural oak, matte white, thin black Heavy gold, dark walnut, ornate styles
Dark walnut / smoked oak Off-white, charcoal, warm rust, forest green Matte black, dark wood, brushed brass Bright white, chrome, heavy ornate
White / lacquered Almost any muted tone — this is the most flexible Matte black, natural birch, simple white Heavy decorative, overly ornate
Mixed wood tones Neutral anchors — greige, warm white, charcoal Consistent frame colour across all pieces Mixing frame materials and colours
Rattan / natural fibres Earthy tones — ochre, clay, sage, warm beige Thin natural wood or no frame at all Black metal, glossy finishes

The mistake I always see is people choosing frames in the wrong wood tone. A pale birch frame on dark furniture looks stranded, and a dark walnut frame on a pale oak console just makes the art look heavy. Match your frame tone to your furniture tone or go to the opposite extreme (matte black with pale wood works brilliantly) — just don't land somewhere in the middle.

[[PRODUCT|minimalist matte black and natural wood frames for Nordic wall art]]
Pro Tip: Keep your frame material consistent across a gallery wall even if the prints vary. Mixed wood tones on a Scandi gallery wall look accidental rather than curated. Pick one frame finish and commit to it.

Room-by-Room Styling Guide for Scandinavian Furniture Pairings

Different rooms have different jobs, and the wall art in each one should reflect that. A Scandinavian living room needs calm and warmth. A Scandi bedroom needs rest and softness. A Nordic kitchen needs practicality with a bit of character.

Here's how I think about it, room by room, using real furniture types and the art that genuinely works alongside them.

[[IMG|room-by-room-scandinavian-wall-art-guide|3:2|photo|Photoreal editorial interior photography, full bleed, calm muted palette, Scandi-minimal styling. Room-by-room art pairings

  • Living room (pale oak sofa frame, linen upholstery): A large-format abstract print in warm grey or dusty sage above the sofa. Go bigger than you think — the low profile of Scandi sofas needs art that fills the vertical space above them confidently.
  • Bedroom (low-profile bed, minimal headboard): Two matching prints in soft tones flanking the headboard — botanical or abstract. Keep them at eye level when seated. Avoid anything too bold or graphic; the bedroom should invite sleep, not stimulation.
  • Kitchen (open shelving, white or wood cabinetry): Small-to-medium prints with a culinary, botanical, or typographic theme. Three prints in a row work better than one large piece here — it echoes the linear rhythm of kitchen cabinetry.
  • Home office (compact desk, birch or white shelving): City map prints or architectural photography feel grounded and purposeful. Avoid overly decorative art in a workspace — it's distracting.
  • Hallway (narrow console, hooks or mirror): A single tall portrait-format print or a vertical trio works brilliantly. The art needs to work quickly since hallways are passed through rather than lived in.
  • Dining area (oval or round table, simple chairs): A generous landscape-format print or an abstract piece in warm neutrals. The scale should feel balanced against the table below it — not dwarfed by it.

I worked with a couple who had a beautiful Scandi bedroom — natural linen, a low oak bed, the works — and above their bed they'd hung a tiny print on its own that looked completely lost. We swapped it for two A3 botanical prints in matching pale wood frames, spaced about 15cm apart, and it immediately felt considered and complete. Scale matters more in Scandi rooms than almost anywhere else because there's so little else going on.

Real Example: In a Scandi kitchen with open white shelves and pale oak worktops, three small botanical prints in a horizontal row — each in a thin matte black frame — works far better than one large piece. The repetition echoes the clean horizontal lines of the shelving above.

Getting this right is what separates a room that feels designed from one that just feels "Scandinavian-ish".

Brand-specific art pairing guide

  • IKEA (KALLAX, BILLY, LACK range): Clean, budget-conscious furniture with a functional, unfussy quality. Pair with bold graphic art, typographic prints, or simple photography. IKEA frames themselves work well here — thin, flat, consistent. This combination looks intentional rather than cheap when you commit to a single frame finish across a gallery wall.
  • HAY: HAY pieces tend to have a bit more playfulness and colour — think soft pastels, rounded forms, and considered details. Art with a slightly graphic or mid-century influence works here. Consider prints with a stronger colour accent — HAY furniture can handle a dusty pink or warm yellow in the artwork where IKEA furniture might be overwhelmed.
  • Muuto: Very refined and material-focused. Art should match that quality — higher-quality paper prints, careful framing, and limited editions feel right. Abstract or architectural photography suits the Muuto aesthetic particularly well.
  • Menu / Audo Copenhagen: Lean towards contemporary and slightly luxurious. Larger format prints, textured papers, and art with a sense of craft — hand-drawn illustration, textured watercolour — sit well with this brand's sensibility.
  • John Lewis Scandi-style ranges: A good middle ground — accessible but considered. Botanical prints, simple photography, and clean abstract work are reliable choices and are easy to find at accessible price points.

Sizing and Gallery Wall Layout Tips for Minimalist Scandi Spaces

Sizing is probably the single most common mistake I see — and it almost always goes the same way: people buy art that's too small. In a Scandi space where the furniture is low and restrained, undersized art looks like an afterthought.

Gallery walls in minimal spaces also need a different approach to the maximalist floor-to-ceiling arrangements you might see elsewhere. The goal is considered, not abundant.

Sizing and layout rules for Scandi gallery walls

  • Above a sofa: Art should be roughly two-thirds the width of the sofa. Go larger before you go smaller. A single print 80–100cm wide works better than two small prints in many cases.
  • Standard gallery wall spacing: Keep gaps between frames consistent — 5–8cm is the sweet spot for a clean, considered look. Wider gaps feel scattered; tighter gaps feel crowded.
  • Odd numbers work: Three or five prints in a gallery wall feels more natural than two or four in most Scandi layouts.
  • Portrait format is your friend: In rooms with lower ceilings — common in UK homes — portrait-format prints draw the eye upward and make the room feel taller.
  • Symmetry or strict asymmetry — nothing in between: In a minimal interior, a near-symmetrical gallery wall that's slightly off looks like a mistake. Either commit to a symmetrical arrangement or make the asymmetry clearly intentional.
  • Lay it out on the floor first: Always. This is non-negotiable. What looks right in your head almost never survives contact with the actual wall until you've tried it flat first.
  • Hang art at eye level: The centre of a single print or the visual centre of a gallery should be at roughly 145–150cm from the floor — standard gallery height and the right choice for Scandi rooms.

We edited it down to three prints in a simple horizontal row, all the same size, same frame, 7cm apart. The wall went from chaotic to considered in about twenty minutes.

Sustainable and Eco-Friendly Wall Art Options Aligned with Nordic Values

Sustainability isn't a trend in Scandinavian design — it's a foundational value that's been part of Nordic culture for generations. If you're furnishing a home with Scandi furniture brands that emphasise responsible production, it genuinely makes sense to apply the same thinking to your wall art.

The good news is that sustainable art options have improved enormously, and the aesthetic difference between eco-friendly and conventional prints is essentially zero now if you choose well.

Sustainable wall art choices for Nordic interiors

  • FSC-certified paper prints: Look for prints produced on paper certified by the Forest Stewardship Council. The visual quality is excellent and the environmental credentials are real.
  • Giclée prints on recycled or cotton rag paper: Higher-quality paper that often feels more premium and ages beautifully — a natural fit for Scandi interiors that value longevity over fast trends.
  • Sustainably sourced wooden frames: Bamboo, reclaimed wood, or FSC-certified timber frames are widely available and align perfectly with the natural materials ethos of Nordic design.
  • Water-based inks: Many quality print producers now use water-based rather than solvent-based inks. Better for the environment and with no perceptible difference in print quality.
  • Textile wall art: Woven or hand-crafted textile pieces made from organic cotton or natural fibres — these are inherently lower-impact and beautifully suited to Scandi interiors.
  • Local and independent artists: Buying directly from a UK-based artist shortens the supply chain significantly. You also tend to get more interesting, less generic work — which suits the Scandi ethos of choosing fewer, better things.
  • Digital downloads: Zero shipping, zero packaging, zero waste. Print them locally on quality paper. Not every option works this way but for typographic or simple graphic prints it's a great approach.

Understanding the deeper principles of Scandinavian design makes every styling decision easier — including your wall art choices.

Scandinavian interior design has always been grounded in the idea that beauty and function aren't opposites — they're the same thing done well. That philosophy shapes everything from furniture construction to the way wall art is chosen and hung.
